title: Black Land, Red Land
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between the fertile valley and the desert around it.
summary: Kemet, the black land, was the narrow strip of Nile silt where Egyptians farmed and lived. Deshret, the red desert, held their cemeteries and guarded their borders.

cards.headline: Ancient Egyptians named their country after its dirt.
cards.body: They called it Kemet, “the black land.” All around it lay a second land, Deshret, red and dry. Where one ended and the other began shaped where Egyptians lived, farmed and buried their dead.

cards.headline: The black land
cards.body: Kemet meant the fertile land of the Nile valley, black with the silt the flood left behind (remember Level 2’s gift?). It was a thin green ribbon. Between Cairo and Aswan, the farmland is mostly just 8 to 16 km wide, and in places only a few hundred meters. At the widest of those usual stretches, you could walk from one edge to the other in an afternoon.

mascot.line: Keep the color code: black for the farmland, red for the desert.

cards.headline: The red land
cards.body: Step off the black soil and you were in Deshret, “the red land”: the hot, dry desert. Cities could flourish only where there was water, in the valley, the Delta or a desert oasis. But the red land had its uses. Its dry climate made it an ideal place for cemeteries. Farm on the black, bury in the red.

cards.headline: A wall made of sand
cards.body: The desert had one more job: it guarded Egypt. Deserts lay to the west and east, the Mediterranean to the north, and the First Cataract of the Nile at Aswan to the south. Historians call it a favorable and secure location. Egypt wasn’t cut off, though: it sat at the center of trade routes to western Asia, the Mediterranean and central Africa. It just had very good fences.

cards.headline: Black and red: sorted
learned: Kemet, the black land: the fertile Nile valley
It was mostly just 8 to 16 km wide
Deshret, the red land: the desert, used for cemeteries
Deserts, sea and cataract gave Egypt secure borders

questions.prompt: Between Cairo and Aswan, how wide is the Nile valley’s farmland in most places?

options.label: Under 1 km
options.rationale: It narrows that much only in places.

options.label: About 100 km
options.rationale: Far too wide: it’s a thin ribbon.

options.label: About 500 km
options.rationale: That would be most of the country.

questions.explanation: The black land is mostly 8 to 16 km wide, and only a few hundred meters in places.

questions.prompt: How did the red land help protect Egypt?

options.label: Its oases held Egypt’s main army
options.rationale: The protection came from the land itself.

options.label: It was lined with walls built by the kings
It flooded every summer, trapping invaders
options.rationale: The flood reached only the black land.

options.label: Deserts to the east and west made Egypt hard to reach

questions.explanation: With deserts on two sides, the sea to the north and the cataract to the south, Egypt had a secure location.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: why did Egyptians call their farmland “the black land”?

options.label: It was covered in dark silt left by the flood
It was burned black before each planting
options.rationale: The color came from the river.

options.label: Its crops were dark in color
options.rationale: It was the soil, not the plants.

options.label: It lay in the shade of tall cliffs
options.rationale: The color came from what the flood left.

questions.explanation: Each year the flood left dark, fertile silt, which gave Kemet both its color and its name.
